analysis.one_liner: Lets tax-exempt churches and charities endorse political candidates without losing their tax break.
analysis.headline: Backed by 38 Republican cosponsors, the bill has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote since its March 2025 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: Current tax law bars churches and other charities from supporting or opposing candidates for office, on pain of losing their tax-exempt status. This bill would lift that bar when the statement fits the organization's usual activities and costs it little extra money. The practical effect is that politically active religious organizations and their donors could put campaign messaging on a tax-subsidized footing, with no disclosure requirement attached.
analysis.who_benefits: Churches and other 501(c)(3) organizations could endorse or attack candidates while keeping tax-exempt status, so long as the statement arises from their regular activities and incurs no more than de minimis extra expense [S2]. The same protection extends to the charitable tax deduction and the excise tax on disallowed campaign spending, meaning donors could keep deducting contributions to an organization that electioneers [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Politically active churches and their donors

how_it_helps.text: A new subsection of the tax code would provide that a charity or church does not lose its exemption, and is not deemed to have participated in a political campaign, solely because of a statement made in the ordinary course of its regular activities that results in no more than de minimis incremental expenses.

The safe harbor also protects the organization for purposes of the charitable deduction and the excise tax penalty on exempt organizations' campaign spending, so donations to an electioneering charity would remain deductible.
The change applies to taxable years ending after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the cost of subsidizing campaign speech through foregone tax revenue, since organizations could electioneer while their donors keep full charitable deductions. Voters get no compensating benefit in transparency: the bill attaches no disclosure requirement, so campaign messaging routed through charities would flow through a channel that does not report political spending.

drawbacks.text: The bill opens a new, tax-advantaged channel into elections: a church or charity could send campaign messaging to its congregation or community while donors deduct their contributions, and neither the organization nor the donor would disclose the political activity.

The limits are vague and hard to police. 'Ordinary course of the organization's regular and customary activities' and 'not more than de minimis incremental expenses' give the IRS little to enforce against an organization that gradually folds candidate advocacy into its regular work, since by definition such statements would incur little extra cost.

The bill does not distinguish between organizations whose mission genuinely requires commenting on public affairs and those that would function as campaign arms, so the main constraint left standing is only the 'de minimis expense' floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain for religious organizations is real but modest, since the existing ban has been loosely enforced and supporters of the bill argue it chills speech that rarely draws penalties anyway. The cost is asymmetric: vague, low limits combined with full deductibility of donor money and no disclosure would let campaign messaging ride on the public treasury through a channel built to be unpoliced.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and has sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Harris (R-NC) introduced the bill on March 31, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
38 Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
No action beyond the original referral appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action.

The bill would amend the tax code so that a 501(c)(3) organization is not treated as engaging in a political campaign solely for statements made in the ordinary course of its activities that cost it no more than de minimis incremental expenses.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet, because nothing has happened. If the bill stays buried, the current rule stands: churches and charities that endorse candidates still risk their tax-exempt status, and taxpayers and campaign-transparency rules are spared a new subsidy channel. Politically active religious organizations and their donors gained nothing so far.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No change yet; current rules stand

for.name: 38 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Democrat joined.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans — 38 of 223 House Republicans signed on, with no Democratic support — and the bill has not advanced past its committee referral.

industries.note: They could endorse or oppose candidates from the pulpit while keeping tax-exempt status, and donors would keep deducting contributions that fund that messaging. The public cost is taxpayer-subsidized electioneering through a channel with no disclosure.
The bill preserves the charitable deduction and excise-tax protections for organizations that electioneer within its limits, so donor money could fund campaign speech at reduced after-tax cost.
They gain the same speech protections, but if their sector becomes a recognized channel for campaign messaging, they face the risk of losing donor and public trust in charitable giving.

analysis.trajectory: Tax bills start in Ways and Means, and with no Democratic support and no committee movement in the months since referral, this one is likely to expire without a vote, as similar proposals to loosen the ban on charity electioneering have in past Congresses.
